articles.title: Trump torches Democrats at Arizona rally, warns they will ‘destroy our country’ ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Trump rallied for Andy Biggs in Bullhead City, blasting Dem Gov. Katie Hobbs and urging Arizona voters to turn the state red in honor of Charlie Kirk.
articles.body: President Donald Trump brought a blunt warning to Arizona voters Wednesday, declaring Democrats would "destroy our country" as he blasted their State of the Union conduct and urged supporters to turn the state red from top to bottom. With Election Day less than three weeks away, Trump rallied behind Rep. Andy Biggs, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, and a slate of GOP candidates during a campaign stop in Bullhead City, taking aim at Democrat Gov. Katie Hobbs and calling for a victory in honor of Charlie Kirk. "On election night, Arizona is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate it," Trump said. "America belongs to those who love, love, love, love — love it." TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG Biggs joined Trump onstage and pointed back to the president’s February State of the Union address to Congress, accusing Democrats of refusing to stand when Trump challenged lawmakers about their commitment to Americans. "Vote Republican top to bottom," Biggs told the crowd. "Let’s turn Arizona red." TRUMP ISSUES BLUNT MIDTERM WARNING; VANCE GREETED WITH ‘48’ CHANTS: TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM GOP CONVENTION Trump seized on the criticism, shifting to lawmakers’ reactions to a veteran honored during the speech. "Not one Democrat smiled or clapped," Trump said. "And that’s when I looked at them, and I said, ‘You people are crazy.’ JOHN FETTERMAN DEFENDS TRUMP SUPPORTERS, CONDEMNS FELLOW DEMOCRATS' 'F--- TRUMP' STRATEGY "But that’s what we have," he continued. "They’ll destroy our country." Trump’s account combined separate moments from the Feb. 24 address. He awarded the Medal of Honor to retired Navy Capt. E. Royce Williams, who was 100 at the time, as Trump recalled Wednesday. He also recognized World War II veteran George "Buddy" Taggart. MICHAEL MONSOOR HAD AN ESCAPE ROUTE; THE MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT CHOSE TO SAVE HIS TEAMMATES INSTEAD The partisan stand-or-sit confrontation came when Trump asked lawmakers to affirm that the government’s first duty was to protect American citizens rather than illegal immigrants. Republicans rose while many Democrats remained seated. Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania separately said he stood to recognize honored guests, including veterans. On Wednesday, Trump also aimed repeated personal attacks on Hobbs, who Biggs is seeking to unseat, calling her a "low IQ individual." BATTLEGROUND DEM GOVERNOR TORCHED FOR ‘DRUNKEN SAILOR’ SPENDING GOP CRITIC SAYS IS SYMBOLIC OF BIGGER PROBLEM Trump praised Biggs’ running mate, former state Sen. Sine Kerr, who is seeking to become Arizona’s first lieutenant governor. Biggs selected Kerr in July for the newly created office. TRUMP FLEXES GOP MUSCLE IN ARIZONA PRIMARIES AS DEMS DODGE FAR-LEFT UPSET Trump also urged supporters to elect Republican secretary of state candidate Alex Kolodin, calling him "a warrior for election integrity" as he attacked Democratic incumbent Adrian Fontes. "You look good. Central casting, actually," Trump told Kolodin, joking that he looked "a little bit nerdy." Trump gave shoutouts to Republican Reps. Paul Gosar, Abe Hamadeh and Eli Crane, describing Hamadeh and Crane as "warriors." He also praised congressional candidate Mark Lamb, calling him "a friend of mine" and urging voters to send him to Washington to represent Arizona’s 5th Congressional District. The rally also included a tribute to Kirk, whom Trump remembered on what he said would have been the conservative activist’s 33rd birthday. "A great person, a great man, a great friend of mine," Trump said as the crowd chanted, "Charlie! Charlie!" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump offered support to Kirk’s widow, Erika, and their family before turning the remembrance into a call to vote. "In Charlie’s honor, we want you to go out and vote," Trump said. "He’d be out there fighting like nobody else. So, let’s have a big victory in honor of Charlie Kirk."

articles.title: Trump says government officials who leak to the media ‘should be shot’
articles.summary: The administration has repeatedly sought to crack down on information leaks to the media.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said at a campaign rally Wednesday that there should be fatal consequences for any government worker who leaks sensitive information to the media. “Leakers should be, in my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump said. “You know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.” Trump described what he said was a planned raid on Iran that he had to call off after someone “leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving.” He appeared to be referring to the U.S. military strike on Iran nuclear facilities in June 2025, which still went ahead. “Somebody leaked, some sleazebag. They ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail, but they leaked that we were leaving at 12:07 from Missouri, and it was in The New York Times, CNN.” “Now, the leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly. They’re real. To me, they’re the scum of the Earth,” he said. Trump, who has called the news media the “true Enemy of the People,” then pointed to the journalists covering his rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, and compared them to leakers. “Those same people up there, they’re almost as bad as a leaker, because they leak,” Trump said. “Oh, they leak false information. That makes them a leaker, right?” Since Trump returned to office, his administration has sought to crack down on information leaked to the media, including proposing to direct federal agencies to have “new and existing employees” sign nondisclosure agreements. Federal investigators subjected about 50 members of the U.S. military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests, pressing them about whether they had shared classified information with journalists, the Times reported last month, citing officials briefed on the move. In January, Trump authorized a search of the home of Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson as part of an investigation into a government contractor who was accused of illegally retaining classified materials. A federal magistrate judge ruled a month later that the administration could not examine the data that FBI agents had seized there. The administration appealed the ruling, but it was upheld by a district court judge. There have been no further appeals. In June, the administration tried to compel testimony from four journalists, three from the Post and one from The Wall Street Journal, before a grand jury, an official familiar with the matter told NBC News at the time. The administration dropped the subpoenas after newspapers pushed back.

articles.title: Group Files Complaint Against Zacharia With Calif. Bar
articles.summary: Group Files Complaint Against Zacharia With Calif. Bar
articles.body:
A government watchdog group filed a complaint Wednesday with the State Bar of California, seeking an investigation into newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia over allegations she falsely represented herself as a lawyer despite apparently never having been licensed to practice.

Campaign for Accountability alleges that Zacharia might have violated California law by repeatedly identifying herself as a lawyer on television and serving as general counsel for a California nonprofit organization.

"If that reporting is accurate, Ms. Zacharia has repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime," the complaint stated.

Rick Coca, a spokesperson for the State Bar of California, confirmed the agency had no record of Zacharia being licensed in California under her married or maiden names.

"Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie," CfA Executive Director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a news release.

"In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime," she said.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung responded on X , calling CfA a "radical-leftist organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome."

"Nobody takes them seriously because they are deranged low lifes," Cheung wrote.

InfluenceWatch, a project of the conservative Capital Research Center, describes CfA as a left-of-center advocacy group that frequently targets Republican officials and conservative organizations.

It notes the group was founded by former staff members of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Government and has two prominent Democrat political operatives on its board.

The complaint cites several instances in which Zacharia described herself as a lawyer, including an Oct. 5 appearance on Newsmax anchor Greg Kelly's WABC radio show, when she invoked her legal background while discussing the Senate's use of blue slips in the confirmation process for U.S. attorneys.

It also questions her reported tenure as general counsel for Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former Trump administration official Richard Grenell, from January 2024 to March 2025.

CfA acknowledged it is unknown whether Zacharia performed legal work for Fix California and asked the State Bar to investigate her responsibilities.

Under California law, unauthorized practice of law or unlawfully representing oneself as entitled to practice law can constitute a misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in county jail, a $1,000 fine, or both.

The complaint asks regulators to consider referring the matter to prosecutors if violations are established.

Zacharia, who graduated from Pepperdine University School of Law in 2011, previously worked for the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing.

Asked Wednesday where she passed the bar exam, Zacharia responded , "when I moved to China."

A White House official told The Hill she worked on international transaction law in China after relocating there with her husband.

President Donald Trump described Zacharia as "an attorney" when announcing her appointment last week.

Material from The Associated Press was used in this report.

articles.title: Trump suggests those who leak government information should ‘be shot’
articles.summary: The US president has long been unhappy with inside information about his administration being leaked to the media.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has suggested that those who leak information to the news media should be shot as punishment.

Trump made the remarks at a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, as he urged supporters to vote in the November 3 midterm elections.

“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump told the crowd. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”

Trump made the statement in an apparent reference to Operation Midnight Hammer, which saw the US launch a surprise attack on Iran in June 2025 during the 12-day war between Israel and Iran.

In the aftermath of the attack, several media outlets published findings from a preliminary report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency.

That report – which had not yet been released to the public – indicated that Iran was able to move some of its enriched uranium away from the sites the US had bombed.

It also suggested that the extent of the damage to Iran’s nuclear facilities was more modest than what Trump had asserted.

Trump, however, appeared to signal that the timing of the US attacks was among the leaked information. He accused the news media of putting military members in danger, calling out The New York Times and CNN in particular.

“They leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving,” Trump said, claiming he had to reschedule the bombing campaign two days later as a result.

“Somebody leaked. Some sleaze-bag, they ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail.”

Trump has long had an adversarial relationship with the news media, and he has previously called for harsh punishment against any official who passes on confidential information to news outlets.

After parts of the Defense Intelligence Agency report became public, he blamed lawmakers in the Democratic Party for its release.

“The Democrats are the ones who leaked the information on the PERFECT FLIGHT to the Nuclear Sites in Iran,” Trump wrote on social media at the time. “They should be prosecuted!”

Under Trump, the White House has taken aggressive action to track down the source of leaks.

Staff in his administration , as well as officers in the military, have also been asked to take polygraph tests.

Journalists at several news outlets, including The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal, have also received subpoenas aimed at determining the sources of internal information made public.

The newspapers had reported on stories such as a botched Navy SEALs raid in North Korea and how Trump ignored internal Pentagon warnings against launching the Iran war.

Last year, the Department of Defense demanded that journalists who wished to access the Pentagon sign an agreement not to publish unauthorised material.

Much of the Pentagon press corps refused to agree, and a federal court struck down many of the new demands made on journalists at the department.

Trump has long raged against leakers, going back to his first term as president from 2017 to 2021.

Former White House official Alyssa Farah Griffin told a podcast in 2024 that Trump had called for leakers to be executed, after media outlets reported that he had taken shelter in a White House bunker during racial justice protests in 2020.

Trump appeared to reprise that sentiment in his speech to Arizona voters on Wednesday, less than three weeks before the November 3 midterms.

“Leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly,” Trump said. “To me, they are the scum of the earth.”

articles.summary: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., and Democrat Cait Conley clashed over ICE enforcement and New York sanctuary laws in a fiery debate that could decide House control in 2026.
articles.body: Rep. Lawler is vying for a third term representing New York's 17th Congressional District, a politically moderate area in the New York City suburbs that could decide the fate of who controls the House of Representatives for the final years of President Donald Trump's term. Lawler called out Conley for misrepresenting his voting record, Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and her own stance on immigration enforcement. Conley, meanwhile, tried to paint Lawler as a Trump acolyte who put the needs of Washington Republicans ahead of the people of his district. DEM CANDIDATE CLEARS CROWDED FIELD TO FACE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT IN NY "I believe that border security is national security and that we do need immigration enforcement to ensure that violent criminals and drug cartels and human traffickers and terrorist organizations aren't in our communities and that they are deported," Conley said. I'll tell you, as a law enforcement officer, you're not permitted to do that kind of stuff." Conley called Gorman's death "an atrocious crime" while repeatedly pointing out it took place in Chicago. Lawler attempted to intervene multiple times to call it "preventable," to which an irate Conley responded, "Can I finish?" "And I do support federal agents and federal law enforcement, federal immigration enforcement, making sure that we deport violent citizens," she said. DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST Lawler then argued, however, that Conley's support of sanctuary policies runs counter to that. "Are you against our small businesses in the Hudson Valley being able to expense their plant, property and equipment and hire more people? Your attack on that rings hollow. You clearly don't understand what's actually in the tax bill. And part of the problem is you don't pay property taxes." Lawler also thanked Conley for her military service. The district is a pivotal one for control of the House next year. Lawler is one of three House Republicans who won a district that former Vice President Kamala Harris also won in 2024. And in an election that's expected to be brutal for the GOP, both sides are pouring millions of dollars into the fight.

articles.title: White House spokesperson Katie Zacharia’s law career faces scrutiny
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia has repeatedly claimed to be a lawyer, but critics question whether she was ever licensed.
articles.body:
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary under United States President Donald Trump, has drawn increasing criticism over claims about her professional background.

On Wednesday, a public accountability nonprofit filed a complaint with the State Bar of California over Zacharia’s repeated claims that she was a lawyer.

If made falsely, such a claim is a crime in the state. According to Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile, she received a degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, but critics have questioned whether she received a licence to practise law, as she has suggested.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the head of the Washington, DC-based Campaign for Accountability, said in a statement. “Yet it seems it was all a lie.”

Her organisation filed the complaint with California’s bar office, a regulatory agency that oversees the licensing of lawyers.

“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” Kuppersmith said.

“The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”

Zacharia, a commentator who has appeared frequently on Fox News and Newsmax, began her term as White House press secretary on Tuesday.

In a news briefing that day, she seemed to falter and speak haltingly, sometimes having to repeat herself.

Her appearance was brief, lasting under 15 minutes. She spent much of her time at the podium thanking Trump for the opportunity and reading from a prepared statement.

“I have wanted to work for him for a very long time,” Zacharia said.

Later, she joined Trump outside the White House to speak further with reporters. When asked where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied, “When I moved to China.”

The response was an apparent reference to a three-year stint in which she claims she worked at a law firm in Beijing.

A biography on the website for the pro-Trump women’s organisation Trumpettes USA Inc says she “served as outside counsel” for the World Bank and International Finance Corporation while in Beijing.

Her LinkedIn profile, meanwhile, indicates Zacharia served as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. More recently, from 2024 to 2025, it lists her as general counsel for Fix California, a voter rights group started by a Trump administration official.

On her Instagram profile, Zacharia describes herself as a “Wife, Mom, & Lawyer”.

But Zacharia’s assertion that she passed the bar in China has fuelled media scrutiny. China’s equivalent of the bar exam, the notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination, can only be taken by Chinese citizens.

China has, on rare occasion, allowed foreigners to practise law in the country if they have several years of experience in their home countries first.

But that does not appear to be the case for Zacharia. According to media reports, Zacharia has not been found to be licensed as a lawyer in any state in the US.

In a statement to The Associated Press, Zacharia responded to the scrutiny by saying, “I practice international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.”

Since Trump’s return to office for a second term, Zacharia has spent several months as a communications adviser at the Department of Homeland Security.

Since June, she has also worked as the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns the Truth Social platform.

articles.title: Suspicious white powder sent to election offices in 3 states
articles.summary: No injuries or adverse health effects have been reported, and officials said they are working with state and federal law enforcement.
articles.body: Secretaries of state’s offices in Ohio, Louisiana and Oklahoma were sent packages this week with mysterious powders, just weeks before the offices are set to oversee the midterm elections. Oklahoma and Louisiana reported receiving the envelopes, while Ohio said U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a package destined for it. The national groups representing secretaries of state and state election directors expressed concern about the suspicious letters in a letter Wednesday. “As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement. “Election officials take these matters seriously and work closely with law enforcement and security partners to protect their personnel and facilities,” the statement added. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose on Wednesday echoed the sentiment that election officials should “never have to fear for their personal safety while performing their duties,” adding that his office was working with state and federal law enforcement following the mailing targeting it. “Fortunately, delivery of the letter was preempted by investigators at the U.S. Postal Service, who are dealing with similar mailings sent to election officials in multiple states,” LaRose said, while thanking the Postal Service. Ohio is one of a few states facing tight elections in just a few weeks. The election bodies of Oklahoma and Louisiana, facing fewer contested elections, were threatened Tuesday, when each state announced it had received packages with suspicious powders. “We want to assure Oklahoma voters that today’s incident does not impact our ability to conduct elections. Election officials remain committed to ensuring safe and secure elections,” Oklahoma State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax said in a statement. Louisiana Secretary of State spokesperson Trey Williams said in an email Wednesday that an employee in the office’s Election Division opened a package containing a white powder and was taken uninjured to the emergency room “as a precaution.” Williams added that law enforcement did not find evidence of “harmful substances.” “Tuesday’s event did not impact any election operations in preparation for the upcoming election,” Williams said. Louisiana State Police said in a statement that it responded to reports of a white powdery substance found in a package at the secretary of state’s office. “LSP is working with the FBI to identify the substance, which was successfully recovered and submitted for testing at the FBI’s crime lab. No employees have reported injuries or adverse health effects related to the incident,” state police spokesperson Jacob Pucheu said in an emailed statement. NBC affiliate KTAL of Shreveport reported Tuesday that the Baton Rouge building was evacuated. The FBI declined in an email to confirm specific instances or locations. The agency said in a statement that it and the Postal Service were “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.” “Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” the FBI’s national press office said. It is not the first time that states’ election officials have faced threats near an election. In 2024, at least 20 states were targeted with letters containing suspicious powders. In one instance in Utah, a mailing with a suspicious powder was intercepted, with a letter signed by a so-called United States Traitor Elimination Army. The mailings prompted several agencies, including the Justice Department, to release guidance about protecting personnel against hazardous materials.

articles.title: White House defends new press secretary Katie Zacharia amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived.
articles.body:
The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.

President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week and she has referred to herself as a lawyer.

But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."

She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".

Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."

On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.

They are seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".

The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.

A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.

The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.

She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.

Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.

A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.

She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.

Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.

In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.

In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.

The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment.

It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.

Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

articles.title: Argentina’s Milei backs Trump for US midterms, calls vote crucial for West
articles.summary: The US President’s ally says conservatives “cannot give an inch” in Latin America as he accepts an award in Washington.
articles.body:
Argentine President Javier Milei has urged his ally, US President Donald Trump, to come out of the United States midterm elections in a stronger position, calling the vote important for the West as a whole.

Milei made the appeal on Wednesday at a Hispanic Heritage gala in Washington, where a Hispanic association gave him an award, ahead of November’s vote.

Conservatives, he said, “cannot give an inch in our reconquest of the hemisphere”, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

Milei flew into the US capital on Wednesday for meetings with investors and the gala. He is due to address the US Chamber of Commerce on Thursday.

Trump firmly backed Milei a year ago, when his government also faced crucial legislative elections. He has called Milei his “favorite president”.

That backing, together with a currency swap agreement with the US Treasury, helped Milei to success in those polls, analysts have argued.

The centrepiece of the package, announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, was a $20bn swap with Argentina’s central bank, in which the US exchanged dollars for pesos. The swap came shortly after Milei’s party lost a key provincial election.

Trump made clear at the time that the support hinged on a Milei victory. “I’m with this man because his philosophy is correct,” he said ahead of a White House lunch with the Argentine leader. “If he wins, we’re staying with him. And if he doesn’t win, we’re gone.”

Trump also warned that the US would not be “generous” if Milei lost. The remarks unsettled Argentine markets, with the main stock index giving up earlier gains and falling about 2 percent, The Associated Press reported.

The package drew criticism in the US. Democratic lawmakers accused Trump of prioritising a foreign bailout while the US government was shut down.

articles.title: Pentagon sends hundreds of Army troops to Latin America for training as drug-trafficking campaign expands
articles.summary: Troops from the 10th Mountain Division are deploying to Panama for jungle training as the Pentagon expands military operations against drug traffickers.
articles.body: The U.S. military is deploying several hundred Army soldiers to Latin America for training and joint exercises with regional forces as the Trump administration expands its campaign against drug-trafficking networks, Fox News confirmed. The deployment involves soldiers from the Army's 10th Mountain Division based at Fort Drum, New York, with the first troops from a roughly 600-soldier battalion expected to deploy to Panama, according to The New York Times, which first reported the deployment. A senior U.S. official confirmed to Fox News that the troops are being forward-staged under U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), which will determine where they are ultimately deployed. According to The Times, the troops will first deploy to a new jungle training facility in Panama before eventually training with local forces in Colombia and Honduras. EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S NEW SECURITY ALLIANCE FACES FIRST REAL-WORLD TEST DEEP IN SOUTH AMERICA AS TROOPS DEPLOY The troops could also support U.S. special operations personnel who are advising local militaries conducting raids against suspected drug traffickers, the outlet reported. Separately, several hundred soldiers from the 10th Mountain Division are expected to help staff a new Western Hemisphere military command based in Miami. The deployment comes as the Pentagon continues military operations targeting suspected drug traffickers across Latin America and the Caribbean. US MILITARY STRIKES ALLEGED NARCO-TRAFFICKING VESSEL IN CARIBBEAN, KILLING 4 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' Since the campaign began more than a year ago, U.S. forces have conducted dozens of strikes, with more than 235 people killed. Gen. Francis Donovan, commander of SOUTHCOM, previously said the military was considering operations against trafficking networks on land. "Do I see land strikes as options? Yes. We want all options at the table," Donovan said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal. "Those actions might be strikes, arrests, or the takedown of a safe house," he continued. "It could even be something as routine as increasing the use of cargo scanners at border checkpoints." TRUMP ADMIN'S LIST OF US-DESIGNATED 'FOREIGN TERRORIST' GROUPS IN LATIN AMERICA EXPANDS TO 21 Donovan added that the goal was to create "total systemic friction" for the cartels. articles.title: Ukraine to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Russia reports a Ukrainian strike on an oil refinery on Thursday, after Ukraine's president says a pause is over following fresh Russian attacks.
articles.body:
Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, Volodymyr Zelensky has said, as he accused the US of withdrawing crucial support.

The Ukrainian president said he had restricted such attacks for three days at Washington's behest, while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times .

Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending the attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and said restrictions to Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate.

The Kremlin said Ukraine had "attempted a large-scale attack" on an oil refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.

According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris had caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.

Zelensky meanwhile said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.

He previously said he would agree to the so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.

But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it agreed to the deal.

Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.

The Ukrainian leader told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".

Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.

After the unexpected restriction to the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection on Tuesday, there were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame. But owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this, suggesting it was the Trump administration 's doing. Trump denied halting intelligence-sharing.

"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.

Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defence told the BBC early on Thursday that Starshield's "operation while on the move" had been restored, referring to the the military-focused version of Starlink.

They said officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances behind yesterday's restrictions".

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?

Starlink restrictions in Ukraine war linked to political situation, Zelensky aide says

Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire

Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv .

European leaders have also rallied around Zelensky, with the matter expected to dominate their summit in Brussels later on Thursday

The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.

Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.

Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Russia's Vladimir Putin.

He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week. "We didn't destroy any relationship."

Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.

Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.

But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.

That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public.

Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."

With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.

Ukrainian officials have said they were not warned before a speed limit was imposed on the Starlink uplink, whose sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US Department of Defense (DoD) contract.

Musk wrote on Wednesday that the systems were owned and controlled by the US government and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [Trump]."

The Trump administration has not commented on the issue. The BBC has approached the White House and the DoD for comment.

articles.title: Woke megachurch pastor, Dem nominee called for repentance over White privilege in wake of George Floyd, BLM
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton once urged his megachurch to repent for White privilege after George Floyd's death as he now challenges Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas.
articles.body: A former pastor and candidate running to make history in deep-red Kansas once suggested that people should repent for their White privilege as protests against the death of George Floyd rippled through the country. During the tumultuous summer of 2020, just days after Floyd’s killing in Minnesota, Adam Hamilton called on his congregation at the Church of the Resurrection to recognize their White privilege and repent. "Like part of what I know is that, is that I grew up in a way that I'm blind to certain things in our society," Hamilton said during a sermon dubbed "Jesus, Protests and Repentance." "I just am. And I have certain benefits by virtue of being educated, White and male, right?" KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’ "And we don't like to hear that, especially White folks don't like to hear that. But there are benefits that come along with that," he continued. Hamilton is running against Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in what has become one of the tightest races of this midterm cycle, despite Kansas' near-century-long history of not sending a Democratic candidate to the Senate. "Roger Marshall wants to talk about anything other than his history of suing and jailing mothers and protecting predators by voting against releasing the Epstein Files," Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton's campaign, told Fox News Digital. "Once again, he’s attacking Adam for something Roger said himself. Roger’s own pastor called Adam ‘middle of the road.’ Kansans are tired of high gas and grocery prices and ready for a senator who won’t divide us by race, religion, income, or ability to pay a medical bill at 18% interest." Republicans acknowledge that they are facing headwinds going into November’s election, but until recently, the contest between Marshall and Hamilton wasn’t of much concern for the GOP. SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL Now, the race has taken a turn and been rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report as voters fume over the cost of fuel, groceries and other economic pain. In response, national Republicans are beginning to dump more resources into the contest to ensure that they maintain the seat. Throughout the race, Marshall has largely aligned himself with President Donald Trump, only rarely breaking from the administration on certain decisions — last month he called for more advance notice and cooperation between the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Kansas government after federal immigration agents descended on the southern part of the state. Marshall has painted Hamilton as a "woke" megachurch pastor, delivering left-leaning ideals from the pulpit. 'JESUS WAS A RADICAL': PROGRESSIVES INVOKE CHRIST TO SELL LEFT-WING AGENDA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL So has an outside group based in Massachusetts, the Main Street Fund, which ran an ad in Kansas that spliced portions of two different sermons and charged that Hamilton was "way too woke for Kansas," shortly after Hamilton won his primary, The Kansas City Star reported. During the sermon from June 2020 amid the Black Lives Matter (BLM) protests, Hamilton pushed back against rioting and looting, and argued that while the BLM movement was the focal point at the time, all lives matters. "Of course all lives matter," Hamilton said. "Everybody understands white lives matter, blue lives matter." Hamilton continued in his sermon posted on the church’s YouTube page in June 2020 amid the Black Lives Matter protests, "When I'm stopped by the police, I'm never afraid that they're gonna pull a gun on me." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But every African American man that I know is worried about what might happen when a police pull him over," Hamilton said at the time. "It's not that all the police are bad, they're gonna do something like that, but there's this fear underneath there. And so the hands go on the steering wheel at 10 and 2. They've been taught that from the time they were children. Right?" "I wasn't taught that, because I don't have to be afraid of that. Right? And there's a whole host of other things that are just a part of life. You know, I can ... well, you get the idea. There are benefits and privileges to my place in life. I have to recognize that," he continued. "To see that. And then I have to listen. I have to listen and understand, and finally be able to see the brokenness in myself, and my indifference. Before I can do anything to help anyone else, I have to have a conversion. I have to repent."And Marshall, who was running for his first term in the Senate at the time, struck a similar somber tone as Hamilton six years ago. In various posts to social media and interviews with local outlets, Marshall condemned Floyd's slaying and pushed for reforms that would ensure what happened in Minnesota and to federal Protective Services Officer Patrick Underwood, who was killed in a drive-by shooting just days after Floyd's death. "Additionally, Republicans called on Congressional Democrats to work across the aisle to make sure that what happened to George Floyd and Patrick Underwood never happens again, and significant bipartisan reform can be passed," Marshall said on Facebook following a House Judiciary hearing on police practices and law enforcement accountability.

articles.title: Mystery surrounds DOJ’s investigation of Gavin Newsom
articles.summary: Nearly four months have passed since California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) publicly and unexpectedly announced President Trump was launching what Newsom described as a politically motivated federal investigation into him and his wife. Federal agents had “knocked on the doors” of family friends and former employees, the governor said at the time. Since then, Newsom…
articles.body:
Nearly four months have passed since California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) publicly and unexpectedly announced President Trump was launching what Newsom described as a politically motivated federal investigation into him and his wife.

Federal agents had “knocked on the doors” of family friends and former employees, the governor said at the time.

Since then, Newsom — widely seen as a 2028 Democratic presidential contender and one of Trump’s most vocal adversaries — has sought to take action. He hired the prominent defense attorney Abbe Lowell and requested the Department of Justice (DOJ) records while seeking to go on offense against Trump’s administration.

Trump, the DOJ and officials representing the administration, for their part, have not said a word on the matter — something Democrats, including Newsom’s allies, find peculiar.

It has left an unusual political standoff between the two sides, with Newsom defending himself against an investigation that has not been officially disclosed.

“I know nothing more than you know. Period. Full stop,” Newsom told reporters late last month when asked if he knew the latest on the DOJ’s investigation. “Never been contacted by anyone, and I continue to make this point. They continue to zig and zag, and I stand by everything I said in my opening remarks on this.”

“They are trying to find something anywhere abusing this process, and it is a disgrace,” the governor continued, before adding, “I know nothing more than you know.”

It’s left Democrats wondering what, if anything, Trump is planning, and how the governor will respond. It also comes as federal agents raided the Washington home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar (Minn.) earlier this week, leaving her property with several boxes of potential evidence.

Last month, The San Francisco Standard obtained federal subpoenas seeking six years of records involving the California State Protocol Foundation.

The foundation — which is funded mostly by corporate donations and is run by a Newsom-appointed board — pays for the governor’s travel expenses. The foundation was created during former California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger’s (R) tenure in order to help cover travel costs by state officials and their aides, and to help spare taxpayers. Every administration since then has tapped into the foundation’s funding.

The foundation has paid for Newsom’s international trips and some trips around the country. The Los Angeles Times reported that in 2020, the foundation paid for Newsom to travel to Miami for Super Bowl LIV. Newsom was there to represent the state when the San Francisco 49ers played in the game.

The Standard reported that the subpoenas issued were for communications involving Steve Kawa — Newsom’s former chief of staff when Newsom was mayor of San Francisco and who headed up the foundation — and Becca Prowda, the wife of San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie. Prowda works at the foundation.

Some Democrats have also speculated that Trump may be trying to tie Newsom to his former chief of staff, Dana Williamson, who earlier this year accepted a plea deal after she was accused of campaign finance fraud, political corruption and tax fraud. Williamson is expected to be sentenced for those federal crimes in December.

Beyond the subpoenas and the political chatter, however, the scope of the investigation remains unclear — including whether prosecutors are examining any wrongdoing by Newsom himself.

A Democratic consultant based in California stressed that the foundation dollars have been used by multiple administrations.

“And if this is about something illegal in the foundation, you would really have to show pay to play,” the consultant said.

“It’s been strange from the beginning,” the California consultant said of the investigation. “The person who is being investigated is releasing the news and the person doing the investigation is quiet.”

A spokesperson for the DOJ did not respond to questions on where the investigation stands.

Newsom has been a frequent critic of the president, regularly going after him on social media, in interviews and speeches. He also led a successful redistricting fight last year in response to a redistricting effort in Texas, which could result in Democrats gaining House seats in California.

After Trump suggested at a rally last week that he would allow Iran to “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego, Newsom led the charge among California Democrats, telling The Hill that the president was “mentally ill” and adding in a statement that it was “TIME FOR THE 25TH!”

Trump has also gone after Newsom on a string of occasions, calling him the worst governor in the country and saying Newsom can’t be president because of his dyslexia, which Trump called a “learning disability.”

Still, the dynamics of any federal investigation of Newsom remain a mystery.

“It’s hard to tell without knowing the details of what’s alleged,” said Gil Duran, who has served as an adviser to California politicians including former Gov. Jerry Brown (D) and the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D). “Even though I’m not a fan of Newsom’s, it’s hard for me to not see this as a weaponization of Trump’s Justice Department.”

Newsom allies agree, saying it’s nothing more than Trump’s efforts to go after his adversaries.

It’s “just another example of Trump’s unethical and illegal use of the Department of Justice to try to harass and tarnish opponents,” said Garry South, who has previously advised Newsom. “He’s too thick and too full of himself to realize that targeting people like Newsom just turns them into heroes among Democrats.”

“No greater honor among Democrats than to have Trump trash you,” South said.

articles.title: Connecticut governor holds double-digit lead in reelection bid: Poll
articles.summary: Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont (D) has a double-digit lead over his Republican opponent Ryan Fazio in the race for the Constitution State’s top job, according to a new poll. In the Emerson College Polling/The Hill survey, 51.4 percent of respondents said they would cast their ballot for Lamont if the election occurred that day or…
articles.body:
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont (D) has a double-digit lead over his Republican opponent Ryan Fazio in the race for the Constitution State’s top job, according to a new poll.

In the Emerson College Polling/The Hill survey, 51.4 percent of respondents said they would cast their ballot for Lamont if the election occurred that day or that they already had cast their ballot for him, while 37.8 percent said the same of Fazio. The poll also found 10.8 percent were unsure about their choice for governor.

Lamont’s nearly 14-point lead comes amid a favorable electoral environment for Democrats as the midterm elections inch closer.

President Trump and Republicans are facing political headwinds including the unpopular war in Iran, the president’s sagging approval rating and concerns about the cost of living.

The Emerson College Polling/The Hill survey also found that 62.3 percent were against Trump’s job performance, while 30 percent were for it and 7.7 were “neutral” or had “no opinion.”

Trump’s nationwide approval rating was sitting at 39 percent on Wednesday afternoon, according to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, with his disapproval rating at 59 percent.

Connecticut is a notably blue state, with the state backing Democrats in every presidential election in 2026 and the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rating Lamont’s race as solidly Democratic.

The Emerson College Polling/The Hill poll took place from Oct. 10 to 12, featuring 800 likely voters in Connecticut and a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points as its credibility interval.

articles.title: Trump, Senate GOP see Starlink become latest flash point over Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine’s sudden and unexplained loss of full access to the military version of Starlink is adding to tensions between President Trump and Senate Republicans as GOP senators are scrambling to find out whether Trump played a role in reducing Ukraine’s defensive capabilities. Many of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters within the Senate Republican Conference stayed silent Wednesday…
articles.body:
Ukraine’s sudden and unexplained loss of full access to the military version of Starlink is adding to tensions between President Trump and Senate Republicans as GOP senators are scrambling to find out whether Trump played a role in reducing Ukraine’s defensive capabilities.

Many of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters within the Senate Republican Conference stayed silent Wednesday after Ukraine revealed it lost critical ability to counter Russian-launched explosive drones because of what a Ukrainian defense adviser, Serhii Breskrestnov, described as a speed limit placed by SpaceX on Starlink terminals.

The news came only a few days after Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release 2.2 million tons of Russian diesel into the U.S. market in a last-ditch effort to reduce domestic diesel prices before the midterm election — a deal Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said left him feeling betrayed.

“It’s pity that we are losing a strong partner,” Zelensky told journalist Piers Morgan in an interview Wednesday.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters within the Senate GOP conference, publicly demanded that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk explain Ukraine’s loss of access to the fast data speeds the country needs for its military operations.

In a social media post Wednesday, Tillis called on Musk to “please tell me these overnight disruptions to Starlink terminals in Ukraine were unintended — that @SpaceX is doing everything it can to fix a temporary glitch.”

Tillis warned that “intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself might be construed as aiding and abetting a mass murderer,” referring to Putin.

“Can you confirm that’s not SpaceX’s intent?” the North Carolina senator demanded.

Starlink is owned and controlled by SpaceX.

Musk then posted to social media a statement explaining that Starlink’s military-linked Starshield systems “are owned and controlled by the U.S. government” and emphasized “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” referring to the president of the United States.

Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s former minister of defense, said Wednesday afternoon that Ukraine’s connectivity with Starlink was being restored at speeds of up to 160 km per hour, allowing it to better track threats.

He thanked Musk for the returned speed and wrote “we hope for your continued support.”

Musk’s statement suggesting Trump would be involved in any decision to limit Ukraine’s ability to access Starshield to track drones and other military vehicles further fueled suspicions on Capitol Hill that Trump might be trying to ramp up pressure on Zelensky to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, which Trump has blamed for the high gas and diesel prices in the United States.

“Reports of Starlink failing in Ukraine are deeply alarming— potentially crippling air defense against Russia’s murderous missiles & drones. Trump & Musk must be held accountable,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who worked closely with Senate Republican colleagues this year to pass a tough new Russia sanctions bill, wrote on social media Wednesday.

Blumenthal and Tillis spearheaded a letter signed by six Republican senators calling on Trump to rescind his deal with Putin to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel into the United States, panning the agreement as “a betrayal of our allies.”

The other Republican senators who signed the letter condemning Trump’s deal with Putin, however — Sens. Mitch McConnell (Ky.), John Cornyn (Texas), Alan Armstrong (Okla.), Susan Collins (Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) — stayed quiet about Ukraine’s inability to access Starlink for a substantial period of time Wednesday.

In their letter to the president Tuesday, the six GOP senators urged Trump to apply more economic pressure on Russia to “enhance” his negotiating position to bring a “swift end” to the “ruinous” conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and emphasized “Putin is a tyrant.”

Two Senate sources said the GOP senators are still digesting the reports trickling out about Ukraine’s loss of full access to Starshield and trying to ascertain why Ukraine’s military suddenly lost the ability to track and intercept Russian-launched drones.

Daniel Fried, the former ambassador to Poland and former assistant secretary of State for European affairs during the Clinton, George W. Bush and Obama administrations, said lawmakers would be reasonable to view Ukraine’s sudden loss of access to Starlink with suspicion.

“Given the fact of the diesel deal and President Trump’s condemnation of Zelensky … the suspicions — while they may not be borne out — are unfortunately reasonable,” he said.

“Pro-free-world senators and members of Congress are right to ask very tough, pointed questions,” he said.

Fried, who is the Weiser Family Distinguished fellow at the Atlantic Council, said “it is appropriate to ask tough questions, and the administration basically has it coming given its mixed messages.”

“The administration has earned this suspicion because of its mixed messages,” he added.

Other Democratic senators also held back from commenting on the controversy as more pieces of information began to emerge.

Moderate GOP Rep. Don Bacon (Neb.) pointed a finger of blame squarely at the Trump administration.

“The Administration’s decision to reduce intel sharing to Ukraine & access to Starlink equates to aiding the invader & the war criminal who bombs cities. Does the Administration think it will get ANY support for the remainder of the 119th Congress? Their agenda is dead unless they change paths,” Bacon warned in a social media post Wednesday.

He reposted a New York Times article reporting that Ukrainian officials and analysts speculated that an order to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starlink’s high-speed data may have come from Washington amid rising tensions between Trump and Zelensky.

Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to get “a new president.”

He warned Saturday that Zelensky “better damn well stop” targeting Russian oil refineries, accusing the Ukrainian leader of wanting “to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.”

Zelensky, in his conversation with Morgan on Wednesday, defended Ukrainian military decisions as driven by critical national security needs.

“We can’t be weak, otherwise we can’t survive,” he continued, suggesting Trump was “choosing” Russia’s side as he tries to broker a peace deal.

“This is our country, it’s our body, our home, our children and this is very important for us,” he said. “That’s why it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we’re okay that he is in the middle.”

“If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle — not on the wrong side. I think his advisers are wrong,” Zelensky argued.

articles.title: Trump’s flood-the-zone strategy drowns state-specific midterm messaging
articles.summary: President Trump is seeking to boost Republican candidates facing tough elections by rolling out a number of key initiatives meant to foster goodwill with voters in battleground states, but he risks overshadowing these announcements with his focus on unrelated issues. Trump touted a South Korean liquified natural gas investment Tuesday during a campaign stop in…
articles.body:
President Trump is seeking to boost Republican candidates facing tough elections by rolling out a number of key initiatives meant to foster goodwill with voters in battleground states, but he risks overshadowing these announcements with his focus on unrelated issues.

Trump touted a South Korean liquified natural gas investment Tuesday during a campaign stop in Alaska for incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The president also made headlines when he pardoned two diesel mechanics — who both pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act — on stage during the rally.

However, during the same event, Trump attacked Texas Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico over the state representative’s recent absence from the campaign trail 3,000 miles away.

On Monday, Trump rallied for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy in Youngstown, where he announced that his administration selected Cleveland to house a Navy submarine component repair center.

But Trump spent much of the rally hammering Ohio Democrats on immigration and alluding to past, unfounded claims about the state’s Haitian community in 2024. The president also used the Ohio rally to lash out at Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

Trump’s unrelated, sometimes eyebrow-raising remarks risk drowning out state economic initiatives meant to boost Republicans as the economy remains an issue for the party ahead of the midterms.

The president made news at a rally in Arizona on Wednesday, telling rallygoers he believes “ leakers should be shot ” and that he originally asked the emir of Qatar if he could borrow a jet to be temporarily used as Air Force One before the emir gifted it to the U.S.

The dynamic is playing out as Republicans are already struggling to message around what seem to be worsening economic indicators less than a month out from the midterms.

Data released Wednesday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed the consumer price index rose 0.6 percent in September and was up 3.7 percent relative to September 2025.

And last month’s jobs report was lower than expected, with only 29,000 jobs added in September.

“It’s hard to fight the headlines sometimes, and right now the latest headlines today are ‘inflation climbed even higher than anticipated.’ And so you’re fighting headwinds, you’re fighting a tough political environment, you’re fighting what people already feel,” said one Republican strategist.

“At the same time, his message isn’t really focused on any of that. It’s a listing of grievances and things I think in an old-school way he felt motivated the base,” the strategist added, arguing that the MAGA base and Republican voters are not getting reassurances from Trump and party leaders on the economy.

The president’s strategy of going off message is nothing new and has worked well for him and his Republican allies to galvanize the base.

“Trump never stays on a consistent message and usually has multiple messages that he delivers that get in the way of each other,” said Ron Bonjean, a Republican strategist.

“In the end what you get is a whole lot of Trump,” he continued.

Voters in states across the country have gotten a whole lot of the president recently as part of his midterm blitz. Just this week alone, the president has held his signature campaign rallies in Ohio, Alaska, Arizona and Montana.

“They’re helpful to try to generate enthusiasm that has been lacking among the base,” Bonjean said. “Getting the president there and focused and show that he still cares about Republicans showing up to vote is helpful.”

“Right now, getting Republicans to the polls is a real urgency,” he added.

However, Bonjean noted Republicans have historically struggled with the risk of turning off independent and swing voters, which is where the economic announcements could come in handy.

“Because of the high gasoline prices and the questions on affordability that Republicans are playing defense on, having these single messages on projects that he’s announcing in states, he would be better focused on that as opposed to trying to make the next wave of national headlines,” Bonjean said.

On top of this week’s announcements in Ohio and Alaska, last week Trump signed an executive order promoting red dye diesel at a rally with Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) as fuel prices wreak havoc on the agriculture sector.

And last month, the president announced in the Oval Office a $15 billion steel plant project for Iowa. GOP Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (Iowa), who is running for reelection, and Ashley Hinson (Iowa), who is running for Senate, were both present for the announcement.

“The president’s economic policies have created thousands of jobs and brought trillions in new investment to communities across America,” said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary at the Republican National Committee.

“Whether it’s a steel plant in Iowa or an LNG [liquefied natural gas] pipeline in Alaska, the president’s policies are putting more money in people’s pockets and delivering real results that will last long beyond the midterms,” she continued.

Art Hackney, an Alaska-based Republican strategist who is supporting Sullivan, said whether Trump’s messaging helps or hurts on the campaign trail does not ultimately matter in Alaska.

“That’s really not the point up here,” Hackney said.

“Alaska is a resource state,” he continued, calling Trump’s Oval Office announcement on the pipeline “dramatically historical.”

After rallying supporters Wednesday in Arizona, Trump traveled to Montana to hold the third rally in his western campaign swing.

When asked in an interview with The Hill what he thinks about Trump’s messaging at rallies, Montana Democratic congressional candidate Sam Forstag said he was focused on economic issues.

“I haven’t had much time to watch his other rallies. It’s been pretty busy out here,” Forstag said ahead of the visit.

“The way I’m approaching it is, I’m talking to people on the ground,” he continued, adding, “People are hurting deeply.”

articles.title: This sparsely populated red state quietly climbed to the top of America's financial rankings
articles.summary: North Dakota tops Truth in Accounting's state finances ranking with a $72,300 taxpayer surplus, while 24 states can't cover all their bills.
articles.body: Of the 50 U.S. states, 24 don't have enough money to cover their bills. Meanwhile, one under-the-radar red state stands apart from the rest, according to a new analysis of state finances. North Dakota ranked No. 1 in Truth in Accounting's 2026 Financial State of the States report, ending fiscal year 2025 with $21 billion more than it needed to pay the state's bills. That financial cushion gave North Dakota the highest "Taxpayer Surplus" in the country at $72,300. The taxpayer surplus figure does not mean that the state's residents receive that amount of money back in their pockets at the end of the year — rather, it represents each taxpayer's share of the state's surplus under the group's methodology. The divide between the states with surplus versus those with burden matters, especially when the economy weakens. States with stronger balance sheets have more room to weather downturns, maintain public services and meet retirement obligations, while states carrying large unfunded debts can face tougher choices over taxes, spending and borrowing when revenues fall. THINK YOUR STATE IS EXPENSIVE? NEW DATA REVEALS WHERE AMERICANS FACE THE HIGHEST COST-OF-LIVING North Dakota's financial position was bolstered by its Legacy Fund, a state investment fund built with oil tax revenue. Although oil, gas and coal tax revenues declined amid lower energy prices, strong investment earnings and federal grant revenue helped offset the drop, according to the report. North Dakota was followed in the rankings by Alaska, Wyoming, Utah and Tennessee. The five states all had taxpayer surpluses ranging from $11,400 in Tennessee to topping out in North Dakota with $72,300. Those handful of states' financial position stands in sharp contrast to nearly half the country. The report found that 24 states did not have enough available assets to cover their financial obligations. New Jersey ranked last, with a $162.3 billion shortfall. Truth in Accounting translates that gap into a $45,800 "Taxpayer Burden," the highest in the country. Connecticut ranked 49th, followed by Illinois, Massachusetts and California. The bottom five states had taxpayer burdens ranging from $16,000 in California to $45,800 in New Jersey. THE RED STATES CHARGING AHEAD WITH AMERICA'S WEALTH AS RIVALS WATCH BILLIONS SLIP AWAY Long-term retirement obligations are a major source of pressure on state finances. Across the country, states had $775 billion in unfunded pension liabilities and $490 billion in unfunded retiree health care obligations in fiscal 2025, according to the report. Despite those shortfalls, most states improved financially in 2025. Strong investment returns boosted pension assets and helped reduce unfunded pension obligations, though Truth in Accounting cautioned that those gains can reverse when markets fall.
