articles.title: Person of interest identified in connection with sexual assault near University of Chicago campus
articles.summary: A person of interest has been identified in connection with a sexual assault that was reported early Sunday morning at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago campus, the school announced Tuesday in a community alert.
articles.body:
CHICAGO ( WGN ) — A person of interest has been identified in connection with a sexual assault that was reported early Sunday morning at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago campus, the school announced Tuesday in a community alert .

The individual is not a University of Chicago student or affiliated with the university and has been banned from campus, the school says. Since the investigation is ongoing and no charges have yet been filed, the identity of the person cannot be disclosed.

According to the university, the identification of a person of interest has been corroborated by witness statements and video evidence from university cameras and license plate readers. All of this information has been shared with the Chicago Police Department, which is leading the investigation, the university says.

Chicago police say a 21-year-old woman — who the school later said is not affiliated with the university — reported to officers that she was sexually assaulted around 2 a.m. Sunday by a male offender inside a residence in the 5600 block of South University Avenue, in Hyde Park on Chicago’s South Side.

The Chicago Maroon , the university’s independent student-run newspaper, first reported that the alleged assault occurred at the house of the Lambda chapter of the Alpha Epsilon Pi (AEPi) fraternity.

A Chicago Tribune report citing CPD’s report on the incident says the victim was dancing at a party at the fraternity house when a man asked her several times to come to a bedroom with him.

She refused, but she went to the bathroom after she began to feel unwell, the report says. The victim said the man then followed her into the bathroom. She lost consciousness, and when she woke up, she said part of her clothing had been removed and she had been sexually assaulted, according to the report.

The report also says witnesses observed three to five people standing outside the bathroom door cheering and encouraging what was happening inside.

A university spokesperson said that after an individual intervened, the suspect fled the house. A community alert was then sent to students Sunday saying the sexual assault was reported to CPD and the University of Chicago Police Department.

The spokesperson also said that “while fraternities are not recognized student organizations at UChicago and thus have no formal affiliation with the university, all university students are subject to university policies and disciplinary procedures. The university remains committed to addressing sexual misconduct cases that occur, to imposing disciplinary consequences as warranted, and to continually improving efforts to prevent sexual misconduct.”

In a statement provided to WGN-TV , a spokesperson for AEPi’s national organization said the fraternity’s headquarters became aware of the incident Sunday afternoon and has since been working with chapter leadership. The spokesperson also said the fraternity chapter is cooperating with university administration and local law enforcement on their investigations.

“Alpha Epsilon Pi Fraternity unconditionally opposes, and its conditions of membership absolutely prohibit, any conduct considered as ‘sexual harassment’ or ‘sexual assault,'” the spokesperson said, in part. “This includes such behaviors as repeated propositioning, coercive pressure, unwanted touching and physical violence.

“… Alpha Epsilon Pi Fraternity unconditionally opposes, and its conditions of membership absolutely prohibit, any conduct considered as ‘sexual harassment’ or ‘sexual assault.’ This includes such behaviors as repeated propositioning, coercive pressure, unwanted touching and physical violence.

“… We have a responsibility to protect each other, our guests, and our community at all times. We must continue to work to uphold that value and ensure that those inside and outside of our organization are made to feel safe. Every AEPi member receives mandatory training on these standards, which staff and volunteers reinforce through chapter visits and national and regional events. Violations may lead to expulsion. AEPi staff and volunteers provide the same oversight and support to chapters whether or not their universities recognize them.”

articles.title: Palatine man charged in alleged mass shooting plot targeting Hindu place of worship
articles.summary: A 19-year-old Palatine man was arrested Sunday after police said he allegedly planned a mass shooting targeting a suburban Hindu place of worship.
articles.body:
PALATINE, Ill. ( WGN ) — A 19-year-old Palatine man was arrested Sunday after police said he allegedly planned a mass shooting targeting a suburban Hindu place of worship.

The Palatine Police Department was contacted by the Mount Prospect Police Department just after 3:30 p.m. Sunday about a potential mass shooting.

Police said a person reported receiving concerning messages from Alexandros Paporakis, 19, of Palatine.

According to police, Paporakis shared a document outlining a plan to carry out a mass shooting. He also sent images of a rifle, rifle magazines, body armor and other tactical equipment.

Police located Paporakis as he was leaving his home in the 1300 block of North Baldwin Court in Palatine and took him into custody.

During a search of Paporakis’ home, police said they found:

Hundreds of rounds of additional rifle ammunition

A tactical vest containing body armor and a patch displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism

During the investigation, with assistance from the FBI’s Chicago Field Office, detectives also found a document titled, “Why I Fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto).”

Police said the document contained statements expressing white supremacist and extremist ideologies, including references to violence against people of South Asian heritage, particularly those of Indian descent.

Detectives believe Paporakis may have been planning to carry out an attack Sunday, possibly targeting a Hindu place of worship in the Aurora area. Police said the specific location has not been confirmed.

Paporakis was charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of weapons.

Paporakis appeared for a detention hearing Wednesday, where a judge ordered him detained. His next court appearance is scheduled for Friday, Oct. 30, at 9 a.m.

The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Palatine Police Department at 847-359-9000 .

Police said there is no ongoing threat to the public.

articles.title: Putin is once again playing Trump for a fool
articles.summary: Xerxes only built one bridge leading to his defeat. Trump keeps building new bridges to Russia after every negotiating defeat at Putin’s hands.
articles.body:
Early Sunday morning, President Trump announced in a Truth Social post that “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine.”

Trump then emphasized that “both parties have agreed” to it and then admonished Moscow and Kyiv to “not break it.”

By noon, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was quoted as telling Axios that “the ceasefire announcement was news for me.” Nonetheless, Zelensky said, “Please tell us when the ceasefire begins; we are ready and we will accept it.”

Late that evening, the Russians weighed in by striking the Combined Heat and Power Plant No. 5 in Kharkiv. They also hit a grocery store, killing three people and injuring nearly two dozen others, including children.

It was as if we were watching a Greek tragedy — Aeschylus’ “The Persians” wherein the opening chorus boasts of Xerxes bridging the Hellespont, only for that same crossing to become the instrument of Persia’s defeat at the hands of the Greeks.

On Monday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov essentially thumbed his nose at Trump, declaring, “Zelensky has not ‘earned’ a respite in hostilities, and Russia will not be taken in by his promises.”

Trump’s hubris had once again led to Russian President Vladimir Putin making fools of him and his special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. By Tuesday, Trump was forced to admit that there had been no ceasefire deal: “They agreed because I said they agreed.”

Ever since Trump publicly berated Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025, with a huge assist from Vice President JD Vance, Putin has effectively played Trump for time as he tries to regain his footing in his faltering military campaign in Ukraine.

Putin did this same thing to Trump during the August 2025 Alaska summit, during which Russia maintained its maximalist negotiating position. He did it again two months later by talking Trump out of sending deep-strike Tomahawk missiles to Ukraine.

Even Trump admitted Putin might be playing him. Yet he continued to let it happen, including when he bought into Russia’s 28-Point Plan last November, effectively endorsing the Kremlin’s illegal seizure of sovereign Ukrainian territory in violation of international law.

Xerxes only built one bridge leading to his defeat. Trump, in contrast, keeps building new bridges to Russia every time Putin outsmarts him.

To date, there has been one common denominator in Trump’s folly. He keeps falling for the fool’s gold being offered up to him by Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy to the U.S. and head of Russia’s Sovereign Fund.

Dmitriev is trying to buy from Trump what Putin’s armies are unable to do on the battlefields of Ukraine: Zelensky’s downfall.

Initially it was Putin trying to buy off Trump. In August 2025, Putin signed a decree during the Anchorage Summit with Trump re-opening the doors for ExxonMobil to “regain [its] shares in the Sakhalin-1 oil and gas project” in Russia.

Thereafter, it was all Dmitriev. In October 2025, he proposed constructing a Bering Strait tunnel connecting the U.S. and Russia. Sensing a potential ally in Elon Musk, he suggested that Musk’s Boring Company be awarded the $8 billion deal.

Late that same year Dmitriev dangled Russian rare earth minerals and gas and oil by offering joint U.S.-Russia Arctic projects. The inducement was aimed at dividing Europe as much as it was leveled at Ukraine. Its funding, in part, was to come from the $300 billion of Russian Central Bank assets currently frozen by the European Union.

In February 2026, Dmitriev decided it was time to go big. His so-called “Dmitriev Package” offered $14 trillion of business deals covering energy, rare earth minerals, Arctic development, and infrastructure projects. Trump only had to stab Ukraine and NATO in the back by forcing Zelensky to cede his country’s Fortress Donbas.

This month, Dmitriev is at it again. He offered a new Nord Stream deal to Kushner and pushed a proposal wherein a U.S.-linked consortium would acquire Russian-owned Lukoil’s international holdings, valued at more than $20 billion.

Ironically, in the spirit of Aeschylus’ The Persians , it was the rapid rise in the price of diesel fuel, due to the U.S. war in Iran, that gave Russia its latest opening to shake Trump down. Desperate ahead of the November midterms, Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russia and to purchase 300,000 tons of Russian diesel.

Bipartisan backlash was immediate. Twelve senators, including six Republicans, demanded that Trump terminate the deal.

Meanwhile, Russia continues bombing Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of winter. Another facility was hit Wednesday, leaving 600,000 Ukrainians without power and in some cases without water.

Trump’s hubris is letting Putin play him. He would be well-served to remember the line from “The Persians” uttered by the ghost of Darius, Xerxes’ father: “For presumptuous pride, when it has matured, bears as its fruit a crop of calamity, from which it reaps an abundant harvest of tears.”

Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the US European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the co-founders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: Why corporate America needs one playbook for a divided Washington after November
articles.summary: Trump's post-2018 playbook proves a Democratic Congress won't sideline his regulatory power, and data center fights are the clearest warning.
articles.body: Data center companies learned the hard way that winning Washington isn't the same as winning the country. They had the permits, the agencies and a president who warned that towns rejecting them would end up "backwards and poor." Then the neighbors showed up. Next month's midterms set the same trap. Polls show Democrats could sweep Congress, and the temptation in every C-suite would be to mistake a Democratic Congress for a Democratic Washington. Companies avoid that mistake when corporate communications and government affairs leaders work hand in hand. Corporate communications staff know that November's vote won't tell you what stakeholders believe about each issue that comes up in the next two years. Government affairs workers know that Congress' flip doesn't mean President Donald Trump is out of power. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT After all, voters sent Republicans packing in 2006, but President George W. Bush still ordered the surge in Iraq two months later and lifted the executive ban on offshore drilling in 2008. President Barack Obama pushed through an immigration order, the Iran nuclear deal and Title IX guidance on gender identity after Republicans took Congress in 2014. And President Joe Biden's Federal Trade Commission kept suing corporations into his final days in office. In each case, congressional power belonged to the president's opponents while the regulatory regime stayed in his hands. And Trump's record shows that he'll use that power. After losing the House in 2018, he did not pivot to the center. He presided over a 35-day government shutdown and then declared a national emergency to fund the border wall. He will make a deal, but on his own terms, and agencies will be his strongest leverage. Any plan that assumes he will spend two years as a quiet lame duck is hoping for a president who has never existed. LEE CARTER: TRUMP CAN STILL GET ATTENTION, CAN HE DISTRACT VOTERS FROM THEIR BILLS? Voters haven't changed sides, either. Voting for Democrats doesn't make voters card-carrying members. The party in the White House has gained House seats just four times in midterm elections since 1900, which means even modest losses are normal. Big losses will be about the most apolitical of all issues: the economy, where the Iran war and tariffs have raised what Americans pay at every gas station and with every grocery order. All of this means that communications and government affairs teams need to think through the stakeholders each group normally tackles alone. Data centers show what happens when they don't. When we studied the industry for Proven Media Solutions' Insider Insights report earlier in October, government affairs teams had spent years winning permits from state and federal agencies and support from elected officials at every level of government. Corporate communications seemed to have been left out of the loop until local communities — passed over for the big important players — played a key role in slowing 40% of data centers that were due to open this year. DATA CENTERS FORGOT THE CONSUMER — AND THAT COULD COST AMERICA THE AI RACE Data centers are the issue du jour, but here are some others that should be considered by both functions at the corporate, division and regional levels once election results are known. Take DEI. Corporations had already long backed off on their most controversial and political aspects with relatively modest pushback, but Trump's early 2025 executive orders put the issue back in the spotlight for months. Government contractors were especially hard hit as words like "equity" were erased from websites — good for contracts but horrible for employee relations, as many felt that diversity had been traded for profit. GOP FRESHMAN FIREBRAND TARGETS GLOBAL CONSULTING GIANT OVER 'PLAINLY ILLEGAL' DEI PRACTICES Should Democrats call some of the large government contractors to testify about these changes, or accuse them publicly of racist behavior, lobbying or behind-the-scenes handshakes won't solve a thing. Corporate communications is going to have to build trust with all stakeholders, especially minority partners, investors and employees — through every possible messenger — before the hearing notice arrives. Or look at immigration, where hotel chains have been under pressure over lodging ICE agents. In January, the General Services Administration removed a Minneapolis-area hotel from federal lodging programs after a Minneapolis-area franchise refused agents rooms. Weeks later, protesters occupied a Manhattan Hilton lobby over the opposite complaint. The chains largely shook off the local controversies, often because they smartly issued statements and then went quiet, but that may be impossible once Congress is involved. It's going to take government affairs relationships with the committees and agencies, combined with corporate communications' read on customers, employees and franchise owners, to navigate these waters. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION That is why the post-election plan needs to be a single playbook, built by both teams, that maps where the company is vulnerable, where it has leverage and which of today's allies could become tomorrow's critics. Government affairs teams know the regulators, agency staff and appointees who will matter no matter who wins. Corporate communications staff know the customers, employees and communities who will judge whatever the company says. A message written for one group will be read by the other, so it has to be the same story every time. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Democrats were supposed to be irrelevant after 2004 and 2024, and the GOP likewise after 2012 and 2020 — and, allegedly, 2026. Voters who want more money in their pockets and data centers nowhere near their backyards are not changing parties, and companies that plan as if they were, will be talking to a country that doesn't exist. articles.title: GOP shrinks ambition despite bashing polls
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Republican actions vs words ▪ Final pre-election inflation report shows spike ▪ Katie Zacharia under fire ▪ Ukraine cut off from Starlink Top Republican officials are downplaying the polls showing their party trailing Democrats across the midterm board even as the GOP is pulling money from certain key states and districts.…
articles.body:
▪ Final pre-election inflation report shows spike

Top Republican officials are downplaying the polls showing their party trailing Democrats across the midterm board even as the GOP is pulling money from certain key states and districts.

National Republican groups have cut their spending in several battleground contests as they prioritize other races with less than three weeks to go.

On the Senate map, the main super PAC that works to elect Republicans to the upper chamber created a big splash earlier this month when it moved money out of North Carolina, pausing a $30 million ad campaign for GOP nominee Michael Whatley , and shifted funds to Kansas. Republican groups have also pulled some money back in Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) is favored to keep his seat.

On the House side, The New York Times first reported Tuesday that Congressional Leadership Fund (CLF), the main super PAC aligned with House Republican leadership, is cutting off financial support for Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (Iowa) and Tom Kean Jr. (N.J.), two of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents.

The group is also withdrawing its ad spending targeting Democratic members that the GOP was hoping to oust, including Reps. Greg Landsman (Ohio) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (Mich.).

Republicans have also pulled back in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District, an area that President Trump carried in 2024, suggesting Rep. Susie Lee (D) is in a strong position to win reelection.

Punchbowl News reported Wednesday that CLF threw in the towel on its efforts to oust Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas), who is running in a district that Texas Republicans specifically drew during mid-decade redistricting to try to increase their chances of defeating him.

These moves come as Democrats have held a steady and comfortable lead in the generic congressional ballot that has seemed to expand in the past month. Polling has suggested they’re competitive in more traditionally red areas in the Midwest and South.

Republican congressional leadership has downplayed the polling, maintaining that Democrats are being overestimated, as has happened in the most recent presidential cycles.

“I’m telling you the polling is wrong,” said Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) during an interview on Fox News. “They have a lot of polling organizations right now acknowledging that they’re under-sampling Republicans because Republicans don’t want to respond to polls anymore.”

As he campaigns for House candidates, Johnson said he’s seeing “huge” energy in the crowds that isn’t being recorded in polling.

“Our candidates are energized, focused and disciplined,” Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), who chairs the Senate GOP’s campaign arm, said in a separate interview on Fox. “We’re going to finish well, stay in the majority, and frankly in states like Minnesota, Michigan and New Hampshire, we are within the margin of error. Striking distance of adding new states to our majority.”

Both Johnson and Scott referenced the possibility of pollsters under-sampling Republicans, producing results that are too skewed in favor of Democrats, a phenomenon known as nonresponse bias.

Decision Desk HQ chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley noted pollsters can use data they have available to determine what turnout should look like and weighting to adjust if they are struggling to reach a certain demographic. Still, it’s not necessarily an easy problem to solve.

“The worse your initial sample is, the harder it is to work your way out of it,” he explained.

Skelley said he is more optimistic about polls being decently accurate given their relative success in the 2018 and 2022 midterm cycles, and improvements in presidential years during the Trump era.

“This is a potential issue. I’m not sure it’s worse now than has been in the past, and it may actually even be better, because if the 2024 polling is any indicator, the polls did do a little better on this with this problem. It doesn’t mean they solved it,” Skelley said.

Analysts told Morning Report the money moves may be even more telling.

“When a party chooses to double down or pull out is a pretty good indication of what they think their chances are,” said Republican strategist Samuel Chen .

Chen said polling data is always up for interpretation, but money suggests how a party is really feeling on the ground.

Democrats have also started to pull their money out of contests like North Carolina’s Senate and New Jersey’s 7th District, where Kean is running, but this comes as the party is increasingly convinced they will win these races.

“They’re going to pull out of places that either are hopeless or are safe. Just like when you pull a quarterback from a football game,” Chen said.

▪ The Hill : Three polls show James Talarico with slight lead in Texas.

More than 70 million Americans on Wednesday learned their Social Security payments will rise by 3.6 percent , as part of the annual cost-of-living adjustment, which is tied to inflation.

The Social Security trust fund is set to run insolvent sometime around 2032, leading to questions about what changes are coming. In our Viewer’s Voice segment, a viewer asked why Congress can’t just raise the cap that currently sets a limit on how much Americans can be taxed. I put the question to Rep. Buddy Carter (R-Ga.).

“That would be very difficult for a number of people to vote for. However, I will tell you that it’s a pretty good idea,” Carter said, if benefits were also increased. “We’ve got to be very careful not to raise taxes. Republicans don’t want to do that,” he added.

While we are focused on the 2026 midterms right now, the debate over how to save Social Security will likely be one of the dominant discussions on Capitol Hill and in elections for years to come.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

The Trump administration’s investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) is aimed at building a case to strip her of her citizenship and ultimately deport her, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday. Officials have reportedly issued more than a dozen subpoenas seeking testimony before a grand jury, including to some of Omar’s relatives.

The Supreme Court sided with Republicans for a second time in a legal battle over TV advertising costs, ruling that the Federal Communications Commission doesn’t need to decide on Democrats’ challenge to its policy of granting political parties access to cheaper rates before the midterms. Lower judges had told the agency to move more quickly with Election Day fast approaching.

A coalition of states is suing the artificial intelligence firm OpenAI over accusations that it has misled users about the safety of its chatbot, ChatGPT. The bipartisan group of eight states allege the company moved forward with developing AI products despite knowing they require safety guardrails.

President Trump speaks at a campaign rally at the Laughlin Bullhead International Airport, Oct. 14, 2026, in Bullhead City, Ariz. (John Locher, Associated Press)

HEATING UP: Soaring energy prices pushed inflation up in September , dealing a blow to Republicans just 20 days before the midterm elections.

The consumer price index rose 3.7 percent relative to September 2025, according to data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics yesterday. Compared with the previous month, prices were 0.6 percent higher, the largest monthly increase in five months.

Gas prices accounted for much of the surge — increasing 34.2 percent over the previous year and 9.1 percent for the month.

The latest inflation report is more bad news for Republicans, who are trying to convince voters to keep them in office, even as voters consistently rank affordability concerns at the top of their priority list and say the president bears responsibility for the high prices.

Only 22 percent of voters approve of Trump’s handling of inflation, while 55 percent say inflation is “not at all” under control, according to a new Fox News poll .

The report has also raised concerns about a potential interest rate jump when the Federal Open Market Committee meets later this month. Investors still predict the next rate hike will wait for December, but the chances of an October increase jumped from 22 percent Tuesday to 44 percent yesterday morning, before falling again to 33 percent by the end of the day, according to CME FedWatch.

Investors will be watching for clues about the Fed’s next move when Chair Kevin Warsh joins Kristalina Georgieva , managing director ofthe International Monetary Fund (IMF),for a fireside chat at the 2026 IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Thailand tonight at 11:30 p.m. EDT.

BACK ON THE TRAIL : Former Vice President Kamala Harris announced a final campaign blitz this fall on behalf of several vulnerable Democrats, as she weighs whether to seek the White House again in 2028.

Her office announced a tour that will take her to several early presidential primary states in the final couple of weeks of the campaign season, from Oct. 21-30. Harris had already announced stops in Georgia and Nevada, but she added appearances in New Hampshire, Wisconsin and Mississippi, as well as a virtual event in Florida. The Associated Press was first to report on the schedule.

The 2024 Democratic presidential nominee has said in recent interviews that she is focused on helping Democrats in 2026, but she has not ruled out a 2028 run for the White House.

HEGSETH, INTERRUPTED: Protesters repeatedly interrupted a major Army convention panel featuring Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to call him a “war criminal” and a “coward” over the administration’s approach to Iran and Gaza.

Hegseth, whose remarks centered on his leadership shake-up in the Army and plans to integrate autonomous systems and drones into the military, made light of some of the interruptions.

“She thinks highly of me,” Hegseth joked, after an audience member called him a “war criminal,” and said, “It appears we have a bit of a tactic,” after he was drowned out by the protesters.

Six protesters were removed by security and local police in Washington, D.C. The National Iranian American Council and CodePink took responsibility for the protests.

The president will participate in a Rose Garden lunch at 12:30 p.m. He will participate in a pre-taped interview at 4 p.m. and tele-rallies at 6 and 6:30 p.m.

The Senate will meet at 9:30 a.m. for a pro forma session.

The House will convene at 11 a.m. for a pro forma session.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press)

BURDEN OF PROOF : White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is under rising scrutiny about whether she passed the bar exam after giving an unexpected answer to a question about her legal background.

The Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint Wednesday with the State Bar of California, asking for an investigation into the new press secretary. The watchdog group argued in the complaint that if Zacharia has presented herself to the public as able to practice law without having a license, it would be a crime under California law.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” Michelle Kuppersmith, Campaign for Accountability’s executive director, said in a statement.

Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile states that she served as general counsel of Fix California, an organization started by Trump administration official Richard Grenell , from 2024 to 2025.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Zacharia sat for the bar exam soon after graduating from Pepperdine’s law school in 2011 but didn’t pass.

Scrutiny surrounding Zacharia emerged quickly after her first press briefing Tuesday morning. Later in the day, she was asked where she passed the bar exam, to which she responded, “When I moved to China.”

She told The New York Times on Wednesday that she misheard the question.

“I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she said over the phone from Trump’s rally in Arizona.

“That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” she added.

Zacharia served as an “associate” at a law firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. But experts told The Hill’s Mallory Wilson that even if Zacharia worked at a law firm in China, that doesn’t necessarily make her a lawyer.

“I don’t believe that she could have taken the Chinese bar exam — American citizens are not, by rule, allowed to sit for it, and there’s no apparent reason to believe that she could have made some special arrangement (if she did, I’d love to learn how she managed that, as it would be extremely difficult),” Taisu Zhang , a professor at Yale Law School who works on contemporary Chinese law and politics, wrote to Wilson.

▪ CNN : White House officials question how long Zacharia can last.

Elon Musk speaks at the SATELLITE Conference and Exhibition, March 9, 2020, in Washington. (Susan Walsh, Associated Press file)

SIGNAL LOST : Ukraine said Wednesday that it suddenly lost access to Starlink’s military system Starshield, prompting concerns about the implications on its air defenses and questions about whether Washington was responsible.

Ukraine’s former defense minister said later in the day that SpaceX was working to restore satellite speeds after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned of dire consequences from the interruption. It was not immediately clear, however, what caused Ukraine to lose access to the space-based communications network or where the order originated.

A source familiar with the matter told The Hill that Starlink services were cut off for objects that traveled more than 100 miles an hour, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk faced pressure to explain Ukraine’s restricted access to Starshield. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said he hoped the disruptions were unintended and SpaceX was“doing everything it can to fix a temporary glitch.”

Musk stressed that his company was not responsible for any decisions that would impact Ukraine’s military capabilities, saying the technology is owned and controlled by the U.S. government and that decisions about limiting usage or speed would be made by the military and Trump.

“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company ,” Musk wrote on social platform X .

And finally … It’s Thursday, which means it’s time for the weekly news quiz!

Kimberly Guilfoyle dominated much of the week’s headlines with the controversy that led to her ouster as ambassador to Greece. So th is week’s quiz will look back at her winding career that’s gone back and forth between media personality and public servant, and a personal life that’s included some high-profile partners.
